transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-25
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 55m
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Patel (Redwood SE), Alex Rivera (Auriga Infra), Priya Singh (Auriga ML), Tom Wu (Auriga CTO)
Links referenced: [deck] https://redwood.ai/s/auriga-kv-deck (shared), KV telemetry template https://redwood.ai/s/kv-telemetry

Summary (auto): Auriga seeing KV eviction + paging spikes on tail latency during sustained long sessions; possible correlation with prefix reuse and session affinity. Discussed prefetch heuristics, TTL vs size-based eviction, and whether quantized models reduce KV footprint enough to avoid thrash.

00:00:02 Maya (Redwood AE): ok thanks everyone for joining, we'll keep to about 55 minutes. quick intros?
00:00:10 Alex (Auriga): alex here, infra lead, running the inference side. we've been hitting some thrash in the kv layer with our customer chat logs.
00:00:18 Priya (Auriga): priya, ml eng, i'm the one who saw the tail blips in our evals.
00:00:23 Tom (Auriga): tom, cto, here to understand tradeoffs and timelines.
00:00:29 Liam (Redwood SE): liam, i'll focus on the runtime / kv details. we pulled your sample traces before this call. note: some names in the traces got munged, so we may ask for clarifying artifacts.

00:02:01 Maya: quick goal for today is to triage the eviction/paging pattern and agree an experimental plan. alex, can you describe the symptoms?
00:02:10 Alex: sure. we have sessions that go long — typically 12k to 25k tokens — and after about 20 concurrent long sessions we start to see token latency jumps, sometimes 3x on p99. the graph looks like repeated spillback events and then recovery.
00:02:33 Priya: we also noticed prefix reuse — many sessions reuse a set of system prompts and user templates, so certain prefixes become hot, but they also get evicted then prefetched repeatedly. feels like prefix thrash.

00:03:20 Liam: got it. couple quick clarifying q's — are you running a quantized model in prod or a full fp16?
00:03:27 Priya: we're on 4-bit quantized LLM in prod (PTQ) and sometimes run an unquantized fp16 baseline in perf tests. the kv footprint per token is smaller with 4-bit but the runtime still shows similar eviction behaviors.
00:03:45 Liam: that's interesting; quantization helps kernel memory but KV (kv cache) is primarily a per-token hidden state store, so the shape changes but not always enough to prevent eviction under certain heuristics.

00:04:30 Tom: is this something that Dedicated would fix? like more memory = less eviction?
00:04:36 Maya: short answer: yes, more capacity helps, but it may just move the threshold — the root cause looks like access pattern: lots of small hot prefixes, high concurrency, plus batching windows that delay KV writes. we should look at policies.

00:05:12 Liam: let me sketch the workflow: requests come in, runtime routes, tokens generate and KV updated; eviction is triggered by combined memory pressure and configured TTL/eviction policy. in your traces we saw frequent small evictions then re-prefetch — that's the thrash.
00:05:39 Alex: we've got autoscaling but the thrash appears before autoscale kicks in; the burst is shorter than scaling window.

00:06:10 Priya: one oddity: when we pinned a handful of prefixes for a control test, p99 improved but throughput dropped slightly. maybe because pinned prefixes occupy memory preventing larger batch sizes?
00:06:28 Liam: correct — pinning reduces eviction but increases steady-state memory committed, which can reduce batch aggregation (smaller effective batch), raising per-token cost/latency. it's a tradeoff.

00:07:05 Maya: we prepared three prefetch heuristic proposals: (A) aggressive prefix pin for top N across org, (B) adaptive prefetch based on session affinity, (C) temporal prefetching for prefixes seen in last T seconds. liam, can you explain the expected effects?
00:07:21 Liam: yeah. A reduces misses for stable hotspots but can starve general cache. B tries to detect session-affine prefixes — if session is likely to reuse, keep its prefixes pinned locally. C is cheaper: simple sliding window prefetch. in your workload, B looks promising because you have long sessions with reuse.

00:08:10 Alex: whats the crash risk of B? complexity and correctness concerns.
00:08:15 Liam: more logic, yes, and you need session identifiers and affinity signals. in Redwood Private or Dedicated behind a VPC it's doable; hosted we can still support but need to verify tokenization of session IDs and privacy constraints.

00:09:00 Priya: how about eviction heuristics? we saw your runtime uses LRU-ish with TTL TTL override options? the docs call it hybrid-LRU-TTL.
00:09:08 Liam: it's a size-aware LRU with a TTL fallback. the TTL by default is kinda conservative; for long contexts it can cause older prefixes to be evicted even if they're likely to be reused. tuning TTL up helps but increases memory pressure.

00:10:02 Tom: and paging? when eviction spills to disk or remote store, what happens to latency?
00:10:09 Liam: when page-to-remote (spillback) happens, you see a large tail; we observed 300-800ms extra per spillback in some traces. paging to disk in private deployments is slower than to remote memory store. if you have SSD-backed local spill it's better than network roundtrips.

00:11:00 Alex: we saw intermittent IOPS saturation on our NFS during a run. could that cause the repeated prefeteches?
00:11:08 Liam: definitely. if your backing store cannot sustain the read throughput, the runtime will retry or block causing backpressure which cascades into batching delays and then more eviction. need to monitor IOPS and latency.

00:12:20 Priya: quantization question — does 4-bit reduce KV persisted size enough to eliminate paging at 20 sessions?
00:12:27 Liam: depends on implementation. PTQ reduces model weights in storage, but runtime often expands to int8/fp16 for compute. The KV cache stores activations; if your quantization pipeline also compresses KV (e.g., 4-bit cache encoding), yes, you can see benefits. Many customers haven't built 4-bit KV encoding; it's an optimization we can enable but it's experimental.

00:13:40 Maya: quick interjection — do we have telemetry fields that Auriga can capture to help us instrument? liam, what do you need?
00:13:47 Liam: key signals: per-prefix access counts, last-access timestamp, size-per-prefix (bytes), spill events with target store + latency, batch window durations, batch sizes, per-token service time, and trace IDs for end-to-end correlation. we've got a telemetry CSV template i'll share.

00:15:05 Alex: we'll gather traces; some of our logs have scrambled tokens due to redaction, hope that's ok.
00:15:12 Liam: that's fine; we mainly need distribution and timing, not raw content.

00:16:00 Priya: about prefetch heuristics — how invasive is B to our runtime config? can we A/B it?
00:16:05 Liam: yes, we can A/B in Redwood Console with rollout policy. B requires session id propagation and a small runtime hook; we can implement it as a canary flag and route a subset of traffic to a canary policy.

00:17:30 Tom: costs — if we pin more prefixes or increase spill buffer, what's the cost delta?
00:17:37 Maya: rough estimate: pinning increases committed memory; on Dedicated it's monthly capacity cost. on Hosted it's per-token + memory premium for reserved slots. we'll run a cost simulation once we have exact prefix sizes.

00:19:00 Alex: any immediate mitigations? we tried increasing TTL but hit more paging eventually. we also tried reducing batch wait windows which reduced p99 but lowered throughput.
00:19:13 Liam: immediate low-risk steps: 1) pin a small set of top-10 prefixes for given service paths, 2) increase spill buffer slightly (if you have headroom), 3) temporarily shorten max batch delay for long-context sessions. each has tradeoffs but can be reverted.

00:21:40 Priya: on the longer term, would enabling a compact KV encoding be suggested? what are the risks?
00:21:46 Liam: compact encoding reduces memory but adds CPU decode/encode overhead which may impact latency if not hardware-accelerated. also, correctness on quantized activations needs validation. it's a good midterm optimization.

00:23:00 Maya: let's talk deployment — Auriga is interested in Redwood Private (VPC). any differences in KV behavior vs Hosted?
00:23:07 Liam: Private gives you control of backing store (local NVMe vs network), you can tune IOPS and local SSD spill which reduces paging latency. Also you can provide HSM/KMS for keys. But ops complexity increases — you manage scaling windows and must plan capacity for spikes.

00:24:30 Alex: we run in GCP with custom NFS — should we move to local NVMe?
00:24:36 Liam: if you can, yes. local NVMe for spill reduces latency and IOPS bottleneck. If not, provision a higher-performance remote memory store (memcached/redis with big instances) and ensure network bandwidth.

00:26:10 Priya: curious about batching windows: how do we tune them without losing throughput? we've seen tiny batch windows improve p99 but hurt throughput.
00:26:18 Liam: it's workload-dependent. suggestions: use adaptive batching that shortens window under high concurrency and lengthens it otherwise; use per-route batching so long-context routes get smaller windows. Redwood Optimize can suggest initial configs based on traces.

00:28:00 Tom: any concerns on security/compliance with session-affinity telemetry?
00:28:06 Maya: we anonymize session ids; in Private you control redaction policies. we won't need PII if you send hashed session ids and timing buckets.

00:29:30 Alex: small nit — some terms in our notes got transcribed as KVcash or K-V cache, hope that didn't change the meaning.
00:29:36 Liam: ha, we've seen KVcash before. it's fine.

00:31:00 Maya: ok, let's propose an experiment pipeline: Auriga provides traces and prefix frequency distribution. Redwood will run three prefetch configs (A,B,C) on a dedicated cluster for a 48-hour run with simulated concurrency. we measure p50/p95/p99, spill events, and cost delta. sound right?
00:31:21 Priya: yes. what about quantization toggle? can we test both 4-bit and fp16?
00:31:27 Liam: yep. we'll run runs with both model variants to estimate KV size change and tail impact. note: when running fp16 you'll need more memory so cost differs.

00:33:10 Alex: timeline?
00:33:12 Maya: deliver telemetry template today; Alex to send traces by 2025-11-30; Redwood runs initial sims and returns results by 2025-12-10; follow-up workshop week of 2025-12-15.
00:33:27 Tom: fine.

00:34:50 Priya: any specific logs you want? we have per-request microsecond stamps and a token-level timeline.
00:34:57 Liam: good — token-level timeline + batch id + prefix ids will help. also include any spike in network latency to backing store.

00:36:10 Alex: we also noticed that certain prefix patterns cause frequent collisions — is prefix hashing causing false grouping?
00:36:18 Liam: could be. our prefix hashing uses a consistent hashing ring to map prefixes to shards; collisions can happen if your prefix namespace is skewed. we can examine your distribution and, if needed, introduce prefix sharding tweaks or add a small pre-hash normalization step.

00:38:05 Maya: okay last technical point — is there a safe way to do a gradual rollout of B (session-affine prefetch) so that we can monitor regression?
00:38:13 Liam: yes: 1) canary 5% traffic with detailed tracing, 2) compare spillback/eviction rates, 3) rollback if p99 regressed. Redwood Console supports this. we'll help set up dashboards.

00:40:10 Tom: cost vs SLA question — if we pin prefixes as a long-term solution, can we get a predictable cost number?
00:40:17 Maya: we'll model memory delta from prefix sizes and multiply by Dedicated capacity pricing. we'll deliver that in the cost sim.

00:42:00 Priya: any known bugs in the runtime kv layer that could cause this besides heuristics?
00:42:07 Liam: we saw a bug in an older runtime release where TTL and reference counting interacted incorrectly under concurrent writes; it was fixed in 2025-06 release. check your runtime version; if you're on pre-2025-06 build that could explain anomalies.
00:42:30 Alex: we're on 2025-03 build.
00:42:34 Liam: upgrade recommended. we'll include a patch note list.

00:44:50 Maya: recapping next steps — I'll send telemetry template; Liam will sketch the three prefetch configs and run sims after we get traces; Auriga to send traces and representative prompts. deliverables and dates noted in next_steps.
00:45:10 Priya: any competitor differences worth noting? i.e., things Anthropic or Vertex do differently?
00:45:17 Liam: some vendors do active KV compression and hierarchical caching (L1 in GPU, L2 in fast nvme, L3 remote), but that adds complexity. Redwood focuses on simple, observable heuristics plus optional compact encoding.

00:47:00 Tom: ok thanks all. wrap?
00:47:04 Maya: thanks everyone. we'll follow up by email with links.
00:47:10 Alex: thanks.

[End of transcript]
